handoff.summary: Batch b03: six atomic biology records (finite rate of increase, one-step and projected discrete geometric growth, empirical Kleiber 3/4 metabolic scaling, sex ratio, complementary allele frequency) grounded in the inspected LibreTexts geometric-growth derivation (Donovan & Welden/Gotelli lineage), OpenStax Biology 2e sections 45.3 and 45.1/19.1, and the inspected Kleiber/allometry summaries. Each record carries two references, domain and missing-input rejections, and inverse notes. Earlier batches' deferred items (continuous models, Kleiber-1932 coefficient) stand unchanged.

assumptions: source assumption: discrete time steps with seasonal, synchronous reproduction (source: the model 'is realistic for many populations that have seasonal, synchronous reproduction').

source assumption: per-capita birth and death rates constant over the modeled period and independent of population size or density (density-independence); the page notes real rates do change and the model is a heuristic starting point valid 'under certain conditions and for limited periods of time'.

gaps: Quantity meanings geometric_rate and finite_rate are not in the runtime vocabulary snapshot; runtime projection omitted.

models.inverse_notes: Geometric rate is recoverable as R = L - 1. Substitution check: L = 1.1 gives R = 0.1, consistent with the published example. Boundary L = 0 (R = -1) means total loss within one interval and is admissible; R < -1 would imply a negative multiplier and is excluded by the guard.
limitations: Names the multiplier implied by a geometric rate; it does not estimate R from field data (that estimation is the separate ratio record family).
Applies only where the discrete-time, density-independent framing holds; continuous breeders need the exponential (exp) family, which is deferred.

references.method: Published example: 'Suppose R = 0.1 individuals/individual/year. Therefore, lambda = 1 + R = 1.1. This implies that the population increases by 10% per year'.
references.provenance: Published result (worked example with exact decimal arithmetic).

references.method: Limiting identity: a zero geometric rate means no per-capita change, so the one-step multiplier is exactly 1 (stable population).
references.provenance: Limiting identity constructed from the definition; not a field observation.

rejection_cases.reason: R = -1.5 would give a negative finite rate (lambda = -0.5), which is meaningless as a population multiplier.
Geometric rate R must be supplied; the multiplier cannot be determined from no input.

relationship.locator: 'Geometric (Discrete-Time) Model' derivation: 'The quantity (1 + R) is often given its own symbol, l (lambda), and its own name: the finite rate of increase.' with worked R = 0.1 -> lambda = 1.1 doubling in about 7.27 years.
relationship.translation_notes: Source symbol lambda transliterated to local L (expression grammar is ASCII-only); R (geometric rate of increase, per-individual per-period) preserved. Dimensional check: pure number 1 plus dimensionless rate gives a dimensionless multiplier. This L is the quantity the assignment's special check calls the discrete per-period multiplier; it must not be confused with the continuous intrinsic rate r (the page stresses 'The parameters r and R are not equal').

sources.evidence: Paraphrase: factoring the one-step equation gives (1 + R), named lambda, the finite rate of increase; R = 0.1 gives lambda = 1.1 (10% per year, doubling about 7.27 years); lambda = 1 + R with r and R explicitly not equal.

assumptions: source assumption: discrete time steps with seasonal, synchronous reproduction and constant density-independent per-capita rates over all t periods (same framing as the one-step record).

source assumption: the multiplier applies at whole-period steps; the page's doubling discussion ('will not quite double in 7 years, and will more than double in 8 years') supports whole-period interpretation only.

gaps: Quantity meanings initial_population, finite_rate and period_count are not in the runtime vocabulary snapshot; runtime projection omitted.

models.inverse_notes: Elapsed periods are recoverable only with logarithms (t = ln(Nt/N0)/ln(L)), which the scalar profile cannot express; that inversion is therefore deferred with the continuous family. The multiplier is recoverable for known t only through t-th roots, likewise out of profile; substitution checks here run the forward direction. Zero-multiplier boundary: L = 0 with t > 0 gives Nt = 0 (extinction within the horizon).
limitations: Whole-period projection only; non-integer t has no within-interval meaning in this framing.
Constant-multiplier projection compounds any rate error exponentially; the source restricts the model to limited periods and heuristic use.

references.method: Published fission series: 'After the third hour, there should be 8000 bacteria'; 1000 * 2^3 = 8000 exact.
references.provenance: Published result (printed census of the fission series) matched by exact integer arithmetic.

references.method: Published series endpoint: 'After 1 day and 24 of these cycles, the population would have increased from 1000 to more than 16 billion'; exact recomputation 1000 * 2^24 = 16,777,216,000 (16.78 billion) is consistent with 'more than 16 billion'.
references.provenance: Published result (page reports the rounded-down magnitude; expected keeps the exact recomputation with a one-individual tolerance).

rejection_cases.reason: A negative elapsed period count has no meaning in forward projection from the initial census.
Elapsed period count t is required; the multiplier alone does not select a horizon.

relationship.translation_notes: Source symbols Nt, N0, lambda, t mapped to local Nt, N0, L, t (ASCII transliteration of lambda). The variable exponent t is a dimensionless period count, so no dimensionful power arises. Dimensional check: count times dimensionless multiplier gives a count. This L is the discrete per-period multiplier and must never be substituted for the continuous rate r (the page: 'The parameters r and R are not equal').

assumptions: source assumption: interspecific comparison of adult resting (basal) metabolic rates across body masses; the regularity is fitted across species, not derived for one individual.

source assumption: FITTED exponent explicitly: approximately 0.75 as the working value, with reported variants 0.73 (Brody 1932), 0.749 (2004 field metabolic rates) and 2/3 fits for small birds and insects; the page states the exponent's exact value is presently unclear and the law 'lacks a single theoretical explanation that is entirely satisfactory', so 0.75 is recorded as the conventional fitted exponent, never as a law of nature.
source assumption: normalization B0 is specific to the taxon group and unit system (70 for kcal/day with mass in kg, 3.4 for watts); it is a fitted input here, not a universal constant.

gaps: Quantity meanings basal_metabolic_rate, metabolic_normalization and body_mass and the mass^0.75 unit are not in the runtime vocabulary snapshot; runtime projection omitted.
Exact Kleiber-1932 printed coefficient unverified (Hilgardia page returned 403); the 70/3.4 normalizations are conventional restatements, which is why B0 is an input rather than a constant.

models.inverse_notes: Mass is recoverable only through the (1/0.75) power, which needs logarithms/roots outside the scalar profile for general inputs; no inverse case is tested. The unit-mass identity runs both ways: M = 1 gives B = B0, and B = B0 with B0 fixed implies M = 1. Zero or negative mass is excluded by the guard (a zero-mass organism has no metabolism to scale).
limitations: An empirical regularity with a contested explanation, not a law: local fits span 2/3 to 3/4 and small species systematically deviate toward 2/3.
Basal (resting) scope only; activity, growth, thermoregulation and taxonomic order shift realized rates (page: most variation is mass-determined but temperature and order matter).
Whole-animal rate only; mass-specific rate (B/M proportional to M^-0.25) is a different quantity and not recorded here.

references.method: Limiting identity: at unit body mass (1 kg) the power term is 1^0.75 = 1, so the predicted rate equals the normalization (70 kcal/day); verifies encoding of the normalization without testing the exponent.
references.provenance: Limiting identity constructed from the definition; not a field observation.

references.method: Published ratio construction: 100^0.75 = 10^1.5 = 31.6228, echoing the page's 'a cat having a mass 100 times that of a mouse will consume only about 32 times the energy' (32 is the page's rounded 31.62); 70 x 31.6228 = 2213.59 in kcal/day.
references.provenance: Value derived from the published 100x-to-about-32x ratio statement; the expected keeps the unrounded recomputation with a 0.01 tolerance.

rejection_cases.reason: Zero body mass has no metabolism to scale and the allometric relation is undefined there.
Normalization B0 is required; body mass alone does not determine the absolute rate.

relationship.locator: Kleiber's law page: 'BMR approx 70w3/4 kilocalories per day, or BMR approx 3.4w3/4 watts (w in kg)' with 'the basal metabolic rate scales to the 3/4 power'; Allometry page: power-law form 'y = k x^a' with a the scaling exponent.
relationship.translation_notes: Conventional 0.75 exponent written as a numeric power per the page's '3/4 power' statement; w transliterated to M, BMR to B, and the normalization (70 or 3.4) generalized to input B0 for the taxon/unit system. Dimensional check: B0 carries the compensating mass^-0.75 so the product is a power (energy/time); the exponent itself is dimensionless. Fitted-vs-theoretical status is explicit in assumptions: 0.75 is the conventional fitted value, not a derived law.

sources.evidence: Paraphrase: basal metabolic rate scales to the 3/4 power of mass; conventionally BMR approx 70 w^0.75 kcal/day or 3.4 w^0.75 watts (w in kg); 100x mass gives about 32x energy; exponent variants 0.73 (Brody), 0.749 (field), 2/3 for small birds/insects; no single satisfactory theoretical explanation.

assumptions: source assumption: a population consists of individuals of one species in one area, and the ratio compares the male and female members of that same population at one time.

models.inverse_notes: Male count is recoverable as M = S * F. Substitution check: 1.5 * 40 = 60, consistent with the unbiased reference. F = 0 is excluded (ratio over zero females undefined); M = 0 gives S = 0 (all-female population), which is admissible.
limitations: A composition ratio only; it carries no information about total size, density or reproductive output.
Operational or effective sex ratios (breeding individuals only) are different quantities and outside this record's scope.

references.method: Constructed illustration: 60 males to 40 females gives 60/40 = 1.5 by direct division; no field value claimed.
references.provenance: Independently constructed arithmetic check at a simple whole-number ratio; not a published field value.

references.method: Admitted ideal boundary: zero males among 50 females gives a ratio of 0, the fully female-biased endpoint.
references.provenance: Definitional boundary check with an explicit compositional meaning.

rejection_cases.reason: A sex ratio over zero females is undefined.

assumptions: source assumption: exactly two alleles at one diploid locus, so the two frequencies exhaust the gene pool (source: 'If these are the only two possible alleles for a given locus in the population, p + q = 1').

gaps: Quantity meaning allele_frequency is not in the runtime vocabulary snapshot; runtime projection omitted.

models.inverse_notes: Symmetric with p = 1 - q; either allele can serve as the known input. Substitution check: q = 0.2 gives p = 0.8, consistent with the violet-flower pair. Endpoints p = 0 (q = 1, fixation of the second allele) and p = 1 (q = 0) are admissible.
limitations: Two-allele loci only; multi-allele systems (such as the ABO example on the same page) need the fuller summation constraint.
A bookkeeping complement, not an equilibrium prediction; it holds regardless of evolutionary forces.

references.method: Published self-check setup: p = 0.8 with q = 0.2; 1 - 0.8 = 0.2 exact.
references.provenance: Published result (printed allele-frequency pair of the worked self-check).

references.method: Figure 19.2 extended description: Y frequency p = .7 with y frequency q = .3; 1 - 0.7 = 0.3 exact.
references.provenance: Published result (printed allele-frequency pair of the figure).

rejection_cases.reason: Allele frequencies are bounded by 0 and 1; p = 1.2 is outside the frequency domain.
Allele frequency p must be supplied; its complement cannot be determined from no input.

relationship.locator: Section 19.1 'Hardy-Weinberg Principle of Equilibrium': 'If these are the only two possible alleles for a given locus in the population, p + q = 1.'
relationship.translation_notes: Normalization constraint solved for q as the single-output serialization; the rearrangement is recorded against this same canonical relationship (no separate record for p = 1 - q). Dimensional check: pure number minus dimensionless frequency gives a dimensionless frequency.

sources.evidence: Paraphrase: with only two alleles at the locus, p + q = 1, comprising all alleles at that locus in the population.
